gloss: seven; swear, bind by oath; a seven, week
summary: שֶׁבַע is seven, the number that orders Israel’s time: the seventh day, seven days of מַצּוֹת and of סֻכּוֹת, seven sabbaths counted to the feast of weeks, the seventh month and the seventh year (Lev 23; 25). שָׁבוּעַ is a seven, a week of days or of years, and חַג שָׁבֻעֹת the feast of weeks (Deu 16:9–10). The same consonants give נִשְׁבַּע “swear” and שְׁבוּעָה “oath”: men swear by Yahweh, and Yahweh swears by himself to Abraham and to David (Gen 22:16; Psa 89:4). Every cognate that keeps the old sibilants apart shows š for “seven”, and the Aramaic verb “swear” shows the same š, so nothing divides the two senses into two roots; but outside Hebrew and Aramaic no language has šbʿ for swearing, and the tie between seven and oath is shown only by scripture’s own use at Beersheba (Gen 21:28–31).

doctrine.statement: God finished his work, ceased on the seventh day, and blessed and made it holy (Gen 2:2–3). Lev 23 builds Yahweh’s appointed times on that seven: the seventh day first (Lev 23:3); seven days of מַצּוֹת with the seventh a holy convocation (Lev 23:6–8); seven sabbaths complete counted from the sheaf, fifty days to the new grain offering (Lev 23:15–16); then the seventh month, holding the day of blowing, יוֹם הַכִּפֻּרִים and seven days of סֻכּוֹת (Lev 23:24, 27, 34–36). The land keeps the seventh year, and seven sevens of years lead to the jubilee, when liberty is proclaimed (Lev 25:4, 8–10); the Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year (Exo 21:2; Deu 15:12). Daniel, reading Jeremiah’s seventy years, is told of seventy sevens determined to finish transgression, make a covering for iniquity and bring in everlasting righteousness, to an anointed one who is cut off (Dan 9:2, 24–26). From the verses: Israel’s calendar repeats the seven of creation on every scale, day, week, month, year and jubilee, and each seven ends in rest, release or covering.

After Abraham offered Isaac, Yahweh said, “By myself I have sworn … I will surely bless you and multiply your seed … and in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed” (Gen 22:16–18), and he renewed that oath to Isaac (Gen 26:3; Psa 105:9). Hebrews explains: because he could swear by none greater, he swore by himself; men swear by the greater, and an oath ends dispute; so God, willing to show the heirs of the promise how unchangeable his counsel is, confirmed it by an oath, that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have strong encouragement (Heb 6:13–18). Zacharias praises God for remembering “the oath which he swore to Abraham our father” in raising up a horn of salvation in David’s house (Luk 1:69, 73). Yahweh swore to David to set his seed on his throne (Psa 89:4, 36; 132:11), and Peter says David, knowing this oath, foresaw the resurrection of Christ (Act 2:30–31). Yahweh swore, “You are a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psa 110:4), and Hebrews makes the oath what sets Jesus’ priesthood above the Levites’, who were made priests without one (Heb 7:20–22, 28). He also swore in wrath that the unbelieving would not enter his rest (Psa 95:11; Heb 3:11, 18–19), and swore by himself that every knee will bow to him (Isa 45:23), which Paul applies to the judgment seat and to the name given to Jesus (Rom 14:10–11; Php 2:9–11). From the verses: the promises on which salvation rests, to Abraham, to David, and of the priest for ever, are not bare promises but sworn by Yahweh himself, and so cannot fail.

From the morrow after the sabbath of the sheaf Israel counts seven sabbaths complete, fifty days, and brings a new grain offering: two loaves baked with leaven, firstfruits to Yahweh (Lev 23:15–17, 20). It is חַג שָׁבֻעֹת, the feast of weeks, of the firstfruits of wheat harvest (Exo 34:22), “the day of the firstfruits … in your weeks” (Num 28:26), counted seven weeks from the first putting of the sickle to the grain, kept with rejoicing by son, daughter, servant, Levite, sojourner, fatherless and widow, remembering that Israel was a slave in Egypt (Deu 16:9–12). “When the day of the πεντηκοστή”, the fiftieth, “was fully come,” the disciples were together, the Holy Spirit was poured out, and men from every nation under heaven heard them speak; about three thousand were added that day (Act 2:1–11, 41). Paul calls believers those who have “the firstfruits of the Spirit” (Rom 8:23), and James says God brought us forth by the word of truth to be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures (Jas 1:18). From the verses: the feast that ended the seven weeks offered the first of the wheat harvest to Yahweh, and on that day the first harvest of the gospel was gathered, by the gift of the Spirit.

The law commands Israel to fear Yahweh, serve him and swear by his name (Deu 6:13; 10:20), and forbids swearing falsely by it, which profanes it (Lev 19:12); swearing by other gods is forsaking him (Jer 5:7; Zep 1:5). Jeremiah requires that one swear “as Yahweh lives” in truth, judgment and righteousness (Jer 4:2), and the psalm’s upright man swears to his own hurt and does not change (Psa 15:4). Jesus takes up “you shall not swear falsely, but shall perform your oaths to the Lord” and says, “do not swear at all … let your yes be yes and your no, no” (Mat 5:33–37), which James repeats (Jas 5:12); he exposes the evasions of swearing by temple or altar as still swearing by God who dwells there (Mat 23:16–22). Put under oath by the high priest “by the living God”, Jesus answers truly (Mat 26:63–64). From the verses: the oath existed to call God to witness one’s word; Jesus asks of his disciples a truthfulness that needs no oath, since every word is spoken before God.

Yahweh set a sevenfold vengeance to guard Cain (Gen 4:15); Lamech boasted, “If Cain is avenged sevenfold, Lamech seventy and seven” (Gen 4:24). When Peter asks whether he should forgive his brother up to seven times, Jesus answers, “Not up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven”, the words of Lamech’s boast, and tells of the servant forgiven a great debt who would not forgive a small one (Mat 18:21–35); if a brother sins seven times in a day and turns seven times, he is to be forgiven (Luk 17:3–4). From the verses: the measure of vengeance Lamech claimed without limit becomes, in Jesus’ teaching, the measure of forgiveness, owed because each has been forgiven far more by God.

note: Drafted 2026-11-11. Seven and swear kept in one entry as asked. What the evidence shows on whether the oath is tied to the number: (a) every cognate that keeps ṯ and š apart (Arabic, Ugaritic, Sabaic, Aramaic) shows š for the numeral, and the Aramaic verb “swear” has ש, not ת, so it too shows š; nothing in the sounds divides the two senses into two older roots. (b) But no language outside Hebrew and Jewish Aramaic uses šbʿ for swearing: Arabic (Lane, root سبع), Ugaritic (Segert’s glossary), Sabaic (Biella; swears with gzm), Punic (Krahmalkov) and Akkadian have only the numeral, and the Jewish Aramaic verb occurs in texts dependent on the Hebrew. (c) Scripture itself ties them: Abraham’s seven ewe lambs as witness and the name Beersheba “because there they swore” (Gen 21:28–31), and Isaac’s well שִׁבְעָה after the oath (Gen 26:31–33). The proposals that נִשְׁבַּע means “to seven oneself”, or to bind by seven things, are explanations, not evidence, and are not stated in the entry. BDB keys: v.av.aa and v.av.ai (Sheba, a man) and v.av.aj (Sheba, a town) share the same spelling-counted tokens; the names are left out (to names/), as are שִׁבְעָה the well (v.av.ab, Gen 26:33, whose tokens are spelling-counted with the numeral), and אַשְׁבֵּעַ (a.gb.ah, 1Ch 4:21, Beth-ashbea). xv.ad.aa (Aramaic שְׁבַע) is likewise spelling-counted, so its 104 uses include Hebrew שִׁבְעָה; the Biblical Aramaic tokens are Dan 3:19; 4:13, 20, 22, 29; Ezr 7:14. v.av.ag (שָׁבוּעַ) also catches Ezk 21:28 and Hab 3:9, which are oaths (שְׁבֻעוֹת), and v.av.al (שְׁבוּעָה) catches Jer 5:24 and Ezk 45:21, which are weeks; the senses cite each under its right word. Ezk 45:21 “a feast of weeks of days” for the Passover is left uncited (text unclear). Hab 3:9 שְׁבֻעוֹת מַטּוֹת is obscure and left uncited. Versification is the Hebrew text’s (Dan 4:13 = English 4:16; Num 30:3 = 30:2; Ezk 21:28 = 21:23; Psa 12:7 = 12:6; Psa 60:9 etc.). Not to be confused with שׂבע (sin) “be satisfied”, a different root key; the Septuagint’s πλησμονή under שִׁבְעָה in the brief belongs to that word, and Punic ŠBʿ I “plenty” and Ugaritic šbʿ “be sated” are its cognates, not this root’s. Peshitta words found from SEDRA lexemes 3106–3108 (root 1808 ܫܒܥ) and the BFBS word list: the Peshitta New Testament has no šbʿ “swear” (it uses ܝܡܐ) and no ܫܒܘܥܐ “week”.
